Iram (duke of Edom)
EYE-ram
proper noun
Hebrew ’iram, “belonging to a city” or “watchful,” the name of the last named of the dukes of Edom in the generations of Esau (Gen 36:43).

Biblical Definition

Duke Iram is the last named of the dukes of Edom, set down at the close of the roll of Esau’s chieftains: Duke Magdiel, duke Iram: these be the dukes of Edom, according to their habitations in the land of their possession: he is Esau the father of the Edomites (Gen 36:43). With this name the long chapter of Esau’s generations is sealed, and the inspired writer adds the solemn summary, he is Esau the father of the Edomites, that no reader might forget the root from whence this nation sprang. Edom is Esau (Gen 36:1,8), the profane brother who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright and found no place of repentance (Heb 12:16–17); and all these dukes and kings, for all their crowns and habitations, are but the seed of him that despised the promise. The chapter ends, and the Spirit of God turns from the genealogy of the rejected to the history of the chosen, from Esau to Jacob, from Edom to Israel. Have not I loved Jacob? saith the LORD: yet I loved Jacob, and I hated Esau (Mal 1:2–3); as it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated (Rom 9:13). Duke Iram closes the line of them whom God passed by; and the closing word, he is Esau, is a warning to every man not to be a profane person, lest he sell an eternal birthright for the pottage of a day.

Webster 1828 Definition

Duke Iram, the last named of the dukes of Edom, after whom the generations of Esau are sealed (Gen 36:43).

IRAM, the last named of the dukes of Edom in the generations of Esau.

He is set down with duke Magdiel at the close of the roll of dukes (Gen 36:43).

After his name the writer adds, he is Esau the father of the Edomites.

His name may signify “belonging to a city” or “watchful.”

He seals the genealogy of the rejected brother, from which the Spirit turns to chosen Israel.

Key Scripture

Gen 36:43 — "Duke Magdiel, duke Iram: these be the dukes of Edom, according to their habitations in the land of their possession: he is Esau the father of the Edomites."

Rom 9:13 — "As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated."

Heb 12:16 — "Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright."

Gen 36:31 — "And these are the kings that reigned in the land of Edom, before there reigned any king over the children of Israel."

Modern Corruption

A duke of the genealogical record whose closing word preaches the profanity of Esau; duke Iram seals the line of the rejected brother and warns against selling an eternal birthright.

expand to see more

Duke Iram is a figure of the sacred register, the last named of the dukes of Edom, after whom the inspired writer sets the seal, he is Esau the father of the Edomites. No movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine him; the dictionary records him that the reader may know him for the close of Esau’s generations, and the turning-point from the rejected line to the chosen.

Here the biblical truth is named plainly in Scripture’s own vocabulary: Esau was a profane person, who sold his birthright for one morsel of meat (Heb 12:16). The closing word, he is Esau, gathers all these kings and dukes under the head of the profane brother whom God passed by: Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated (Rom 9:13; Mal 1:2–3). The principle to recover is the sovereign distinguishing love of God in election, and the warning that no man barter an eternal birthright for the pottage of a day.

Hebrew Roots

From the Hebrew for “belonging to a city” or “watchful,” Iram names the last duke of Edom, who seals the generations of Esau.

Usage

"Duke Iram seals the line of Esau, and the closing word is, he is Esau."

"All the kings and dukes of Edom are but the seed of the profane brother."

"Let no man sell an eternal birthright, as Esau did, for the pottage of a day."
